title.text: Giving a model your knowledge: retrieval-augmented generation, long context and fine-tuning

objects.text: How do I give an AI model my company’s knowledge, and when is each way worth it?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 9 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to Session 9. A model knows what it learned in training and what you put in front of it. It has not read your handbook, your contracts or your price lists. Today you see three ways to change that, in the order a sensible company tries them, and you see real numbers from real runs on a handbook.

By the end you can say which way fits a request from your own job.

title.text:
Your two hours: three ways to
give a model your knowledge

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_d5b0938c.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Thirty-five minutes of ideas, twenty-five of demonstrations, and a paper exercise.

slides.notes:
Today answers one question: how does a model get to know your company?

We start with a short recall of Session 8. Then comes the main part: a ladder of three ways, prompt first, then retrieval, then fine-tuning, with a picture and a real number for each. After that I run three demonstrations on the handbook of Nile Valley Foods. You then work through a paper exercise without a computer, and we finish with what this means for your own job.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  Name three parts of a strong prompt.
2.  Why ask a model for structured output?
3.  How does a reasoning model differ from a standard model?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 8. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Name three parts of a strong prompt. Take a moment.

A good answer is this. A role, the context, the task, examples and the output format; and you test the prompt on a checked set.

Question two. Why ask a model for structured output? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. The answer can then be checked and used by the next step without retyping.

Question three. How does a reasoning model differ from a standard model? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. It spends extra effort working through the problem before it answers. You frame the problem clearly rather than dictate every step.

If an answer was missing, your own task card or last workbook page has it. Now to today.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A search step that fetches the right passages before the model answers. Short for retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG.
One piece of a document, cut so that it can be searched.
A list of numbers that stands for the meaning of a text.
How much text a model can read at one time.
Extra training that changes the habits of a model. LoRA is a light way to do it.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Retrieval. A search step that fetches the right passages before the model answers. Short for retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG.

Chunk. One piece of a document, cut so that it can be searched.

Embedding. A list of numbers that stands for the meaning of a text.

Context window. How much text a model can read at one time.

Fine-tuning. Extra training that changes the habits of a model. LoRA is a light way to do it.

title.text:
A model knows only what it learned
and what you put in front of it

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_knowledge_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A model knows only what it learned and what you put in front of it

objects.text: Your handbook was never in its training.

runs.text: Training stops at a cut-off date.
Your files stay unseen unless you supply them.
It may refuse or guess. You check which.

slides.notes:
Think of a new accountant who has just left university. Clever, well read, and with no idea what your company decided last March. A model is in the same position. It learned from a huge amount of text up to a cut-off date. Your handbook, your price lists and your contracts were never part of that.

So today is about a single question: how does the model get to see your knowledge?

There are three ways, and they differ in cost and in what they can do.

title.text:
Three ways to give a model your
knowledge, from cheapest to dearest

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_ladder_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Three ways to give a model your knowledge, from cheapest to dearest

objects.text: Source for the order: one vendor guide, checked 6 November 2026. See the notes.

slides.notes:
Here is the ladder for the whole session. Rung one is the prompt: you paste what the model needs. Rung two is retrieval: a search step fetches the right pages first. Rung three is fine-tuning: extra training that changes the model itself. Each rung costs more effort than the one below.

One vendor guide, from OpenAI, also says to start with prompting and a set of at least twenty checked questions, and to move up when the cheaper step falls short. That is advice from one vendor, and the logic is general: measure first, then climb.

title.text:
Rung 1: paste the page. The
handbook is only 1,074 tokens

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_tokens_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Rung 1: paste the page. The handbook is only 1,074 tokens

objects.text: A short document fits in a prompt, and no extra tooling is needed.

runs.text: A token is a piece of a word.
829 words came to 1,074 tokens, about 1.3 a word.

slides.notes:
Rung one costs nothing but care. If the answer lives in one short document, paste it into the prompt and ask. I counted the real tokens of four NVF documents with a standard counting tool. The staff handbook excerpt is eight hundred and twenty-nine words and ten hundred and seventy-four tokens.

That is about one and a third tokens a word. Models differ in how they count, so treat the figures as an order of size. Before you build anything, ask whether pasting would do.

title.text:
Rung 2: retrieval works like a
librarian who fetches the pages first

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_librarian_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Rung 2: retrieval works like a librarian who fetches the pages first

objects.text: Real run on the NVF staff handbook: all-MiniLM-L6-v2, 6 November 2026.

slides.notes:
Picture a library. You do not give the reader the whole building. A librarian takes your question, finds the three most relevant pages and puts them on the desk. Retrieval does exactly that. The question becomes numbers, an embedding. Every chunk of the handbook has numbers too. The system scores each chunk against the question and fetches the top three.

The model then writes the answer from those pages only. In this real example, clause three point two scores zero point seven three and the answer is the Finance Manager.

title.text:
Where you cut the document
decides what the librarian can find

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_chunks_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Where you cut the document decides what the librarian can find

objects.text: A chunk is one piece of the document. Cut badly and a rule is split in two.

runs.text: By clause: 30 chunks, 8 of 8 right.
Every 150 characters: 5 of 8 right.

slides.notes:
Chunking is the quiet step that decides a lot. I ran the same eight questions three ways. Cutting by clause kept every rule whole, and the top hit held the whole answer in eight of eight questions. Cutting every one hundred and fifty characters split clause three point two in half, the answer sat in the second piece, and the top hit was the first.

That gave five of eight. Cutting every three hundred characters also gave eight of eight on this small file. So the lesson is to look at your chunks, and test.

title.text:
A score says how close two
meanings are: 0.73 beats 0.47

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_scores_q03_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A score says how close two meanings are: 0.73 beats 0.47

objects.text: This is the cosine similarity from Session 4, now used to rank clauses.

runs.text: 1.00 means identical meaning.
Gap for Q03: 0.73 minus 0.47 is 0.26.
The top three go to the model.

slides.notes:
Now the real term. Each score here is a cosine similarity, the angle idea from Session 4. A score of one means identical meaning. For the question about who approves a claim of UGX 1,500,000, clause three point two scores zero point seven three. The next clause, about receipts, scores zero point four seven.

The gap is zero point two six. The system keeps the top three and hands them to the model. These are the real numbers from the run.

title.text:
Demonstration: the retrieval step
on all ten handbook questions

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_retrieval_table_7.30x3.90.png
objects.alt: Demonstration: the retrieval step on all ten handbook questions

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: 8 of 8 answerable questions: the right clause comes first
Q08 scores only 0.40 and is still first
Q09 scores 0.70 and has no answer

slides.notes:
This is a real run you can repeat. I cut the handbook into thirty clauses, embedded them and the ten questions, and listed the closest clause for each. For the eight questions that the handbook answers, the right clause came first every time. Question eight, about accommodation, scored only zero point four zero, and it was still first.

Watch the last two rows. Those questions have no answer in the handbook, yet question nine still scores zero point seven zero. Keep that in mind for what follows.

title.text:
The closest page is not always an
answer, so let the model say so

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_miss_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The closest page is not always an answer, so let the model say so

objects.text: A high score means the topics are close. It does not mean the answer is there.

runs.text: Q09 asks for paid sick days. The handbook does not say.
0.70 for leave clause 2.1, against 0.73 for the real answer to Q03.

slides.notes:
Here is a retrieval limit you must know. Question nine asks how many days of paid sick leave staff get. The handbook gives no number. Yet the closest clause, annual leave, scores zero point seven zero, almost the same as the zero point seven three for a question that does have an answer.

So a score alone cannot tell you whether the answer is present. In the recorded runs the assistant read the pages and wrote not stated. That is why your instructions must allow that answer, and why you test it.

title.text:
The same questions with no handbook,
three clauses, and the whole text

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_with_without_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The same questions with no handbook, three clauses, and the whole text

objects.text: Scored on the answer key. Recorded runs: Claude, fresh sessions, 4 and 6 November 2026.

slides.notes:
This is the same question with and without the document, as recorded runs. With no handbook text, the assistant said not stated for all ten questions, in two runs, and it invented nothing. That earns two right answers, only because questions nine and ten are really not stated.

With three retrieved clauses it scored ten of ten in two runs. With the whole handbook pasted in, ten of ten in two runs. These are fresh Claude sessions, not ChatGPT or Gemini, and another product may behave differently.

title.text:
Measure each rung on ten checked
questions before you climb

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_measure_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Measure each rung on ten checked questions before you climb

objects.text: Use the same ten questions and the same key every time.

runs.text: Two of ten here is two honest "not stated" answers.
A rung earns its place only if it moves this score.

slides.notes:
This is the habit that stops waste. Keep ten questions with known answers; the vendor guide suggests twenty or more for a serious test, and ten is a workable start. Run them with the cheap step, then with the next step, and compare. On this set the runs with no handbook scored two of ten, and those two are only the questions where not stated is the right answer.

Pasting the text or retrieving three clauses scored ten of ten. So on this set the cheapest step that works is pasting or retrieving, and fine-tuning would add nothing. Your own set may say something different. Session 10 turns this into a routine.

title.text: Long context lets you paste a lot, but it has limits

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_context_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Long context lets you paste a lot, but it has limits

objects.text: The context window is everything the model reads at once.

runs.text: Researchers report that facts in the middle of a long input can be missed.
Longer input costs more and takes longer.

slides.notes:
Many models now accept long inputs, so you can paste a whole contract or a whole handbook. That is rung one stretched. It has limits. A published study by Liu and colleagues found that models often used information at the start and the end of a long input better than information in the middle.

That was in the tests they ran, so I draw the shape and give no numbers. Longer inputs also cost more and take longer, and everything you paste is sent to the model, so check the data rules from Session 13 first.

title.text: Paste the whole document, or retrieve the pieces?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_doc_0.75.png

objects.text: Paste everything

runs.text: One short file, like a 1,074 token handbook
Easy to set up
Answers use the whole text

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.75.png

objects.text: Retrieve the pieces

runs.text: Many files, or files that change
Only the top chunks are sent
Needs chunking and a test set

objects.text: Paste what fits and still answers well. Retrieve when it does not.

slides.notes:
So which one?

If your knowledge is one short file, paste it. Anthropic makes the same point in its write-up on retrieval: for a small knowledge base you can simply put it all in the prompt. If you have hundreds of files, or files that change every week, retrieval keeps the prompt small and the cost down, and it can point to the source clause.

It needs more care: chunking, scores and a test set. The decision is empirical. Try the simple way, measure, and climb if it falls short.

title.text:
Rung 3: fine-tuning trains a
new hire in the house style

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_lora_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Rung 3: fine-tuning trains a new hire in the house style

objects.text: A new hire reads 48 model replies and picks up the way we write.

runs.text: LoRA freezes the model and trains thin added tables.
Here: 294,912 of 124,439,808 weights, or 0.24 percent.

slides.notes:
Fine-tuning is training a new hire. You do not give the hire the handbook each morning. You show forty-eight model replies, and the hire learns the greeting, the length and the sign-off. LoRA is a light way to do it, from a 2021 paper by Hu and colleagues.

It freezes the original weights and trains two thin tables added to them. In my run on a small open model, only two hundred and ninety-four thousand nine hundred and twelve weights were trained, which is zero point two four percent of the total.

title.text:
Demonstration: a tiny LoRA
learns a house sign-off

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_before_after_7.30x3.90.png
objects.alt: Demonstration: a tiny LoRA learns a house sign-off

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Sign-off present: 0 of 6, then 6 of 6
Style is learned
Facts are invented: "Monday" and the name

slides.notes:
This is a real run of a tiny experiment on a small open model called GPT-2, with forty-eight invented replies in one house style. Before training, none of six new messages got the house sign-off, and the text wandered. After training, all six ended with the sign-off. Now read the replies.

The model promised to arrive on Monday and greeted a Ms Nye, and nobody told it either. Other replies invented a cancellation on Wednesday. It learned the style. It did not learn facts. The model is tiny and the data is invented, so this shows the idea, not what a real product would do.

title.text: Retrieval supplies facts. Fine-tuning shapes habits.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.75.png

objects.text: Use retrieval for

runs.text: Facts that change
Answers that cite a clause
Private documents

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_gear_0.75.png

objects.text: Use fine-tuning for

runs.text: A steady format or tone at volume
A task the prompt cannot teach
Examples you own and may use

objects.text: Fine-tune only after the prompt and retrieval measurably fall short.

slides.notes:
The demonstration gives the rule. Retrieval supplies facts: the model reads the page and can cite the clause. Fine-tuning shapes habits: a tone, a format, a way of working. The same vendor guide I mentioned says use retrieval when the model lacks knowledge, and fine-tuning when output is inconsistent or the format is wrong.

It also warns that the methods can be combined, but only if each earns its place. And the examples you train on must be yours to use, with personal data removed.

title.text:
Choose the rung for six
requests from Nile Valley Foods

objects.text: 25 minutes
Hands-on, no computer
Pick prompt, retrieve or fine-tune for each request, and say what test would show the cheaper rung falls short.

Write P, R or F for each, with one line of reason.
Write the ten-question test you would run first.
Compare with a partner or with me.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_5.50x3.55_1812023f.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: A completed rung sheet and one test you could run next week.

slides.notes:
Now your turn, on paper. Your worksheet has six requests from Nile Valley Foods, from summarising one email to answering staff questions from a changing handbook. For each, choose prompt, retrieve or fine-tune and give one line of reason. Then write the ten questions you would use to test the cheaper rung first.

Work alone for fifteen minutes and then compare with a partner or with me. If you disagree, the useful question is what measurement would settle it.

title.text:
Where would each rung
help or hurt in your own job?

objects.text: Which request in your job needs your knowledge, and which rung does it need?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_doc_0.80.png

objects.text: Prompt only
One short document or a few rules, pasted each time

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.80.png

objects.text: Retrieve
Many or changing documents, and answers that cite the source

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_gear_0.80.png

objects.text: Fine-tune
A steady style at volume, with examples you may use

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.80.png

objects.text: Test first
You have no checked questions yet, so write ten
Write the request, your chosen rung and the ten-question test you will write.

slides.notes:
Take fifteen minutes with your own work. Pick one request where the model needs your knowledge: a policy question, a contract clause, a supplier price, a reply in your house style. Which rung does it need?

Prompt only, if one short document will do. Retrieve, if the documents are many or change. Fine-tune, if the style is the problem and you hold examples you may use. Or test first, if you cannot yet say how you would know the answer is right. Write the choice and the reason.

title.text:
Take-away: three questions, asked in
this order, before you build anything

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_tree_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Take-away: three questions, asked in this order, before you build anything

objects.text: Keep this page. Session 10 shows how to run the test set.

slides.notes:
This is the page to keep. First, does a clearer prompt with the page pasted in give right answers on your ten questions?

If yes, stop. Second, are the facts too many, too long or changing?

Then retrieve, and look at your chunks. Third, is the style or format still wrong after the first two?

Then consider fine-tuning, with examples you own. At every step you measure on a checked set before you climb. Next time we see how models fail, and how to check them.

title.text: Keep the decision tree: climb one rung at a time

objects.text: What you keep from today

runs.text: A one-page decision tree: prompt first, then retrieve, then fine-tune, and the test that tells you when to climb.

objects.text: Our question today
How do I give an AI model my company’s knowledge, and when is each way worth it?
Next session
Session 10: When models fail, and how to check them. Optional: note one AI answer at work that you were not sure about.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_card_4.10x4.50_2782c13a.png

slides.notes:
Take the one-page decision tree and keep it next to your own list of requests. The rule is simple to say and hard to follow: prompt first, then retrieve, then fine-tune, and climb only when the cheaper step measurably falls short. Next time we look at how models fail and how to check them, and the ten questions we used today become your test set.

We began with this question: How do I give an AI model my company’s knowledge, and when is each way worth it? Before you go, say in one sentence what you can now say about it.
